newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee co-ops gang up to join exporters.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee co-ops gang up to join exporters.

text.p: A group of four co-operatives and one co-operative association is forming a trading company which hopes to be one of the country's leading coffee exporters, said the head of one of the co-operatives involved.
The company, to be known as Trading Coffee Sul de Minas, should be running as early as next month, said Gilson Ximenes, who is also president of the growers' National Coffee Council.

The four co-operatives involved are at Tres Pontas, Boa Esperanca, Varginha and Sao Sebastiao do Paraiso while the cooperative center in Varginha which represents 18 smaller cooperatives also is part of the pool.
Together the cooperatives have access to three million 60-kg bags, Ximenes said.
The company will have offices in Varginha and Santos, with a likely candidate already identified to head the trading operations, he added.
As well as exporting coffee, the group will import goods such as fertilizers and machinery, Ximenes said.
Cooperatives have in the past made various forays in the form of exporters.

The most successful currently is Cooxupe cooperative in Guaxupe, southern Minas Gerais state, which was the fifth largest exporter in calendar year 1996 according to statistics from the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation.

Cooxupe last week opened a new warehouse in Monte Carmelo which can house 165,000 bags and which, using a facility alongside, will allow the cooperative to seal coffee at origin before it is taken in containers to Santos for export.
Some exporters, while waiting to see how successful the most recent cooperative venture is, are slightly concerned about the impact on their own business.
"The way cooperatives have worked in the past is if they have a beter offer in the internal market, they completely forget about the external market," one dealer said.
"But people are still a bit worried about this new venture," he added.
However an exporter representative was less openly concerned about the prospect of a new player on the market.
"We've had many attempts in the past of producer-oriented companies getting involved. I think any competition is to be welcomed," said Febec president Oswaldo Aranha.
